title: The Coin That Wrote a Warning on Its Edge
topic: The Coin That Wrote a Warning on Its Edge
mechanism: Hand-hammered silver coins had ragged edges, so a clipped sliver went unseen; machine-struck coins carry a lettered edge (DECUS ET TUTAMEN), so one cut breaks the sentence and any thumb can feel the theft.

beats.hook: Scissors bite into a silver coin's rim, a sliver of silver flies at the lens; the clipper grins; the sliver drops into a jar with a clink.
beats.story: A 1690s London clipper snips slivers off ragged hammered coins in his candlelit garret and spends the coins at full value.
beats.rise: His jar of silver grows; he even jokes to a customer; the crier calls in the old coins, and he plans the same trick on the shiny new machine-struck ones.
beats.twist: The baker's thumb runs around the edge of his clipped new coin and stops at a gap: the lettering reads DECUS ET TUT. The door bangs open: men from the Mint. In the Tower, Isaac Newton waits.
beats.mechanism: Inside the Mint: an OLD HAMMERED coin with a ragged rim next to the MILL press and the EDGE DIE rolling DECUS ET TUTAMEN round the rim; a cut sliver leaves the sentence broken; thumbs become guards; the recoinage done in three years.
beats.ending: Today a modern ridged coin rolls out of a pocket and spins to a stop; final word: Safeguard. The last frames run back into the scissors of the first shot.

seed.what: The Tower of London (where the Mint is) seen through the clipper's window, and the shiny new coin's lettered edge

gags.what: The jar overflows and silver dust puffs into the clipper's face; he sneezes.
The scissors skid off the ridged edge and snap shut on the clipper's thumb.
The door bangs open; the clipper dives under the counter and knocks over a tray of loaves.

format_note: Coins are drawn about 2-3x real size in macro shots so the edge lettering reads on a phone. The catch at the bakery is a dramatisation of why the lettered edge works, not a documented arrest.
